prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Handbook of Methods Consumer Price Index Overview

Consumer Price Index: Overview

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a representative basket of consumer goods and services. The CPI measures inflation as experienced by consumers in their day-to-day living expenses. Indexes are available for the United States and various geographic areas. Average price data for select utility, automotive fuel, and food items are also available. CPI indexes are used to adjust income eligibility levels for government assistance, federal tax brackets, federally mandated cost-of-living increases, private sector wage and salary increases, poverty measures, and consumer and commercial rent escalations. Consequently, the CPI directly affects hundreds of millions of Americans.

Quick Facts: Consumer Price Index
Subject areas Prices
Key measures
  • Average prices
  • Consumer price indexes
  • Consumer prices
How the data are obtained Survey of households, Survey of businesses
Classification Commodity
Classification system

CPI entry level items (ELIs)

Scope Urban consumers
Sample sizes

CPI survey collects about 94,000 prices and 8,000 rental housing units quotes each month
Reference Period

Monthly
Revision Information

Final when issued, except for C-CPI-U

  • Consumer Price Index news release

Consumer Price Index: Calculation

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by consumers for a representative basket of consumer goods and services. The CPI measures inflation as experienced by consumers in their day-to-day living expenses. The CPI is used to adjust income eligibility levels for government assistance, federal tax brackets, federally mandated cost of living increases, private sector wage and salary increases, and consumer and commercial rent escalations. Consequently, the CPI directly affects hundreds of millions of Americans.

In the CPI, the urban areas of the United States are divided into 32 geographic areas, called index areas. 29 U.S. Code § 2 - Collection, collation, and reports of labor statistics

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes
prev | next

The Bureau of Labor Statistics, under the direction of the Secretary of Labor, shall collect, collate, and report at least once each year, or oftener if necessary, full and complete statistics of the conditions of labor and the products and distribution of the products of the same, and to this end said Secretary shall have power to employ any or either of the bureaus provided for his department and to rearrange such statistical work, and to distribute or consolidate the same as may be deemed desirable in the public interests; and said Secretary shall also have authority to call upon other departments of the Government for statistical data and results obtained by them; and said Secretary of Labor may collate, arrange, and publish such statistical information so obtained in such manner as to him may seem wise.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics shall also collect, collate, report, and publish at least once each month full and complete statistics of the volume of and changes in employment, as indicated by the number of persons employed, the total wages paid, and the total hours of employment, in the service of the Federal Government, the States and political subdivisions thereof, and in the following industries and their principal branches: (1) Manufacturing; (2) mining, quarrying, and crude petroleum production; (3) building construction; (4) agriculture and lumbering; (5) transportation, communication, and other public utilities; (6) the retail and wholesale trades; and such other industries as the Secretary of Labor may deem it in the public interest to include. Such statistics shall be reported for all such industries and their principal branches throughout the United States and also by States and/or Federal reserve districts and by such smaller geographical subdivisions as the said Secretary may from time to time prescribe. The said Secretary is authorized to arrange with any Federal, State, or municipal bureau or other governmental agency for the collection of such statistics in such manner as he may deem satisfactory, and may assign special agents of the Department of Labor to any such bureau or agency to assist in such collection.

(Mar. 4, 1913, ch. 141, § 4, 37 Stat. 737; July 7, 1930, ch. 873, 46 Stat. 1019.)
Editorial Notes
Amendments

1930—Act July 7, 1930, inserted second par.

Statutory Notes and Related Subsidiaries
Census Data on Women-Owned Businesses; Study and Report

For provisions requiring Bureaus of Labor Statistics and the Census to include certain data on women-owned businesses in census reports, and requiring a study and report on the most cost effective and accurate means to gather and present such data, see section 501 of Pub. L. 100–533, set out as a note under section 131 of Title 13, Census.

Consumer Price Index for Older Americans

Pub. L. 100–175, title I, § 191, Nov. 29, 1987, 101 Stat. 967, provided that:

“The Secretary of Labor shall, through the Bureau of Labor Statistics, develop, from existing data sources, a reweighted index of consumer prices which reflects the expenditures for consumption by Americans 62 years of age and older. The Secretary shall furnish to the Congress the index within 180 days after the date of enactment of this Act [Nov. 29, 1987]. The Secretary shall include with the index furnished a report which explains the characteristics of the reweighted index, the research necessary to develop and measure accurately the rate of inflation affecting such Americans, and provides estimates of time and cost required for additional activities necessary to carry out the objectives of this section.”
Prison Statistics Report

Joint Res. June 17, 1940, ch. 389, 54 Stat. 401, authorized Bureau of Labor Statistics to furnish a report to Congress before May 1, 1941, on kind, amount, and value of all goods produced in State and Federal prisons.

Executive Documents
Transfer of Functions

For transfer of functions of other officers, employees, and agencies of Department of Labor, with certain exceptions, to Secretary of Labor, with power to delegate, see Reorg. Plan No. 6 of 1950, §§ 1, 2, 15 F.R. 3174, 64 Stat. 1263, set out in the Appendix to Title 5, Government Organization and Employees.

Average Price Data (AP)
					ap.txt

Section Listing

1.  Survey Definition
2.  FTP files listed in the survey directory
3.  Time series, series file, data file, & mapping file definitions and relationships
4.  Series file format and field definitions
5.  Data file format and field definitions
6.  Mapping file formats and field definitions
7.  Data Element Dictionary

===================================================================================
Section 1
===================================================================================

The following is a definition of:  Average Price Data (AP)

Survey Description: Average consumer prices are calculated for household
fuel, motor fuel, and food items from prices collected for the Consumer
Price Index (CPI). Average prices are best used to measure the price level
in a particular month, not to measure price change over time. It is more
appropriate to use CPI index values for the particular item categories to measure
price change.

Prices, except for electricity, are collected monthly by BLS representatives
in the 75 urban areas priced for the CPI.  Electricity prices are collected
for the BLS for the same 75 areas on a monthly basis by the Department of
Energy using mail questionnaires. All fuel prices include applicable
Federal, State, and local taxes; prices for natural gas and electricity also
include fuel and purchased gas adjustments.

Summary Data Available: Average consumer prices for household fuel and
motor fuel are available for the U.S. city average, 23 urban areas, 4
regions, 12 region/size class groupings, and 9 divisions.

Average consumer prices for food are available for the U.S. city average, and
four regions. 

Monthly data are available for up to 6 household fuel categories, 6
motor fuel categories, and around 100 food categories.

Frequency of Observations: All data are monthly; annual averages are not
available.

Data Characteristics: Average prices are stored to three decimal places.

Updating Schedule: Updates become available with the monthly release of new data, typically from the 10th to the  14th of the month
following the reference month.
====================================================================================
Section 2
====================================================================================
The following Average Price Data files are on the BLS internet in the sub-directory 
pub/time.series/ap:

	ap.data.0.Current		- All current year-to-date data
	ap.data.1.HouseholdFuels	- All household fuels data
	ap.data.2.Gasoline		- All gasoline data
	ap.data.3.Food			- All food data
	ap.area				- Area codes		mapping file
	ap.contacts			- Contacts for ap survey  
	ap.footnote			- Footnote codes	mapping file
	ap.item				- Item codes		mapping file
	ap.period			- Period codes		mapping file
	ap.series			- All series and their beginning and end Dates
	ap.txt				- General information
	
=================================================================================
Section 3
=================================================================================
The definition of a time series, its relationship to and the interrelationship
among series, data and mapping files is detailed below:

A time series refers to a set of data observed over an extended period of time
over consistent time intervals (i.e. monthly, quarterly, semi-annually, annually).  
BLS time series data are typically produced at monthly intervals and represent data 
ranging from a specific consumer item in a specific geographical area whose price 
is gathered monthly to a category of worker in a specific industry whose employment
rate is being recorded monthly, etc.

The FTP files are organized such that data users are provided with the following
set of files to use in their efforts to interpret data files:

a)  a series file (only one series file per survey)
b)  mapping files
c)  data files

The series file contains a set of codes which, together, compose a series 
identification code that serves to uniquely identify a single time series.  
Additionally, the series file also contains the following series-level information:

a) the period and year corresponding to the first data observation 
b) the period and year corresponding to the most recent data observation 

The mapping files are definition files that contain explanatory text descriptions
that correspond to each of the various codes contained within each series
identification code.

The data file contains one line of data for each observation period pertaining to a
specific time series.  Each line contains a reference to the following:

a) a series identification code
b) year in which data is observed
c) period for which data is observed (M13, Q05, and S03 indicate annual averages)
d) value
e) footnote code (if available)
=================================================================================
Section 4
=================================================================================
File Structure and Format: The following represents the file format used to define
ap.series.  Note the Field Numbers are for reference only; they do not exist in the
database.  Data files are in ASCII text format.  Data elements are separated by 
spaces; the first record of each file contains the column headers for the data 
elements stored in each field.  Each record ends with a new line character. 

Field #/Data Element	Length		Value(Example)		

1.  series_id		  17		APU0000701111

2.  area_code		   4		S100

3.  item_code		   7		712211

4.  begin_year		   4		1980

5.  begin_period	   3		M01		
				
6.  end_year		   4		2002		

7.  end_period		   3		M02

Code					Value(Example)

seasonal(code)		=		U
area_code		=		0000
item_code		=		701111
==================================================================================
Section 5
==================================================================================
File Structure and Format: The following represents the file format used to define
each data file. Note that the field numbers are for reference only; they do not 
exist in the database.  Data files are in ASCII text format. Data elements are 
separated by spaces; the first record of each file contains the column headers for 
the data elements stored in each field. Each record ends with a new line character.  

The ap.data file is partitioned into four separate files:  

	1.  ap.data.0.Current		= All current year-to-date data
	2.  ap.data.1.HouseholdFuels	= All household fuel (fuel oil,
					  utility gas, electricity) data
	3.  ap.data.2.Gasoline		= All gasoline data
	4.  ap.data.3.Food		= All food data

Both of the above data files have the following format:

item_code		=		701111
============================================================================
Section 6
============================================================================
File Structure and Format: The following represents the file format used to define
each mapping file. Note that the field numbers are for reference only; they do not

separated by tabs; the first record of each file contains the column headers for the

Section 7

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
Description: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services. Indexes are available for the U.S. and various geographic areas. Average price data for select utility, automotive fuel, and food items are also available.
URL: https://bls.gov/cpi

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Consumer Price Index (CPI): research and preservation report

**Research date:** October 8, 2026  
**Authoritative publisher:** U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), U.S. Department of Labor  
**Canonical program website:** https://www.bls.gov/cpi/

## Executive assessment

**Your title, description, and URL are accurate.** The description closely matches BLS’s own explanation of the Consumer Price Index.

The most important qualification is that **“CPI” is a statistical program and a family of datasets—not a single downloadable table.** It includes several population-specific indexes, thousands of geographic and expenditure-category time series, average-price series, research indexes, weights, methodological documentation, and historical releases.

The CPI is foundational public infrastructure. It supports inflation monitoring, benefit and tax adjustments, wage bargaining, contract escalation, and research into purchasing power. Its preservation value is exceptionally high because changes to its estimates, methods, or availability can affect both economic interpretation and actual payments.

**Priority findings for researchers and preservationists:**

- Preserve **data together with series metadata, weights, methods, footnotes, and release dates**.
- Distinguish CPI-U, CPI-W, and chained CPI; they are not interchangeable.
- Distinguish **seasonally adjusted** from **not seasonally adjusted** observations.
- Preserve publication versions: some CPI products are revised.
- Do not assume an uninterrupted monthly record. **The October 2025 all-items CPI observation is missing because of a federal shutdown.**
- BLS announced significant collection reductions in 2025.
- Public aggregate statistics are freely reusable, but underlying respondent-level price observations are confidential.
- The BLS restricted-data availability table consulted for this report marks **CPI researcher access as suspended**.

Sources: [BLS CPI overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/home.htm), [CPI databases](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/data.htm), [shutdown-related release changes](https://www.bls.gov/bls/2025-lapse-revised-release-dates.htm), [restricted-data availability](https://www.bls.gov/rda/what-datasets-are-available.htm).

---

## 1. Dataset identity and recommended catalog description

| Catalog element | Finding |
|---|---|
| Official title | Consumer Price Index (CPI) |
| Creator and publisher | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics |
| Parent department | U.S. Department of Labor |
| Resource type | Continuing statistical program; aggregate time-series databases and supporting publications |
| Subject | Consumer prices, inflation, purchasing power, household consumption |
| Geographic scope | United States urban consumer population; national and selected subnational statistics |
| Temporal scope | Selected national series extend to 1913; individual series have different start dates |
| Principal frequency | Monthly; some local series are bimonthly, with additional annual and semiannual products |
| Principal units | Index points; percent changes; dollars per specified unit for average-price data |
| Public access | Free access to published aggregate statistics |
| Reuse status | BLS-published statistics are public domain; separate restrictions apply to protected images and agency emblems |
| Underlying microdata | Confidential, not an unrestricted public-use dataset |
| Persistent identification | BLS series identifiers identify individual time series; the program homepage is not a version-specific data identifier |

### Suggested catalog abstract

> The Consumer Price Index is a family of statistical measures produced by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics that estimates average changes over time in prices paid by urban consumers for consumer goods and services. Principal products include the CPI for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), and Chained CPI for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). Published data include national and selected subnational indexes, expenditure-category indexes, average prices for selected food and energy products, expenditure weights, and research series. Population coverage, geographic detail, reference bases, publication frequency, and revision policies vary by series.

**Cataloging recommendation:** Create a collection-level record for CPI, with separate records or distributions for CPI-U, CPI-W, C-CPI-U, average prices, research series, and archived releases. Do not describe the collection simply as “monthly U.S. inflation.”

Sources: [CPI overview](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/overview.htm), [Handbook overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/home.htm), [copyright policy](https://www.bls.gov/opub/copyright-information.htm).

---

## 2. Publisher, institutional responsibilities, and legal authority

### Who produces it?

BLS is responsible for CPI statistical design, price collection, estimation, analysis, and publication. Its CPI program operates within the agency’s consumer-prices organization.

Other organizations supply important inputs:

- **U.S. Census Bureau:** population and geographic information; collection of the Consumer Expenditure Surveys for BLS.
- **Consumer Expenditure Surveys (CE):** household spending information used to construct expenditure weights and identify shopping outlets.
- **Businesses, service providers, landlords, and tenants:** prices and housing information.
- **Administrative and alternative data providers:** information used for selected categories.

The CPI should therefore be understood as a product of several interdependent statistical systems, not merely a survey of retail prices.

Sources: [CPI FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm), [data sources](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/data.htm).

### General statutory authority

The principal collection authority cited in CPI survey materials is **29 U.S.C. § 2**, “Collection, collation, and reports of labor statistics.”

It authorizes BLS, under the Secretary of Labor, to collect, collate, and report statistics about labor and the products and distribution of labor. CPI respondent materials explicitly identify this provision as their legal authority.

**Important distinction:** This is broad statistical authority. It should not be described as a standalone “CPI Act” prescribing the entire modern index formula. The same section contains a monthly employment-statistics requirement, but that language should not be mistaken for a detailed CPI-specific publication mandate.

Sources: [29 U.S.C. § 2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2), [CPI respondent material hosted by Reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/DownloadDocument?objectID=99146401).

### Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

CPI respondent collections are subject to Office of Management and Budget clearance.

- The **CPI Commodities and Services Survey** uses **OMB control number 1220-0039**.
- Respondent materials describe cooperation as **voluntary**.
- Clearance documents provide useful evidence about burden, collection procedures, staffing assumptions, costs, and changes in operations.

A 2026 renewal record consulted for this report cites 29 U.S.C. § 2 and shows the collection undergoing OIRA review. Because OMB approval status and expiration dates change, preservationists should retain the actual clearance record associated with each collection period.

Source: [2026 clearance record, reproduced by OMB.report](https://omb.report/icr/202604-1220-001). OMB.report is a secondary mirror, not the authoritative government publisher.

### Specific mandates and legally required uses

Separate laws require or govern particular CPI-related products and applications:

- **Older Americans’ index:** Public Law 100-175, § 191, enacted November 29, 1987, directed the Secretary of Labor to develop a reweighted consumer-price index reflecting expenditures by Americans age 62 and older.
- **Social Security:** The Social Security Act’s cost-of-living provisions use CPI-W in determining automatic benefit adjustments.
- **Federal income taxes:** **26 U.S.C. § 1(f)** specifies inflation-adjustment rules and defines C-CPI-U for relevant tax adjustments.

These are **mandates for a particular product or use**, distinct from BLS’s general authority to collect statistics.

Sources: [older-Americans mandate in statutory notes](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2), [tax statute](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/1).

### Confidentiality law

Identifiable respondent information is protected under the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (CIPSEA)**, now codified in relevant provisions of Title 44.

BLS promises statistical use and protection against identifiable disclosure without informed consent. Protected confidential information is not made public simply because someone submits a Freedom of Information Act request.

Source: [BLS CIPSEA implementation report](https://www.bls.gov/bls/cipsea-report.htm).

---

## 3. What data products exist?

### Principal index families

| Product | What it represents | Important distinction |
|---|---|---|
| **CPI-U** | All Urban Consumers | Broadest principal CPI population; covers over 90% of the U.S. population |
| **CPI-W** | Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers | Subset of CPI-U, approximately 30% of the population; used for Social Security COLAs |
| **C-CPI-U** | Chained CPI for All Urban Consumers | Uses expenditure information to account more fully for substitution across categories; subject to revision |
| **Average-price data** | Dollar prices for selected food, motor-fuel, and household-energy products | Price levels, not quality-controlled inflation indexes |
| **Research indexes** | Alternative populations, methods, or historically more consistent measures | Not automatically substitutes for statutory or contractual CPI series |

CPI-W eligibility depends on household income and employment criteria, not just whether someone receives wages. CPI-U also includes urban retirees, unemployed people, self-employed people, and professional workers.

Sources: [CPI FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm), [research-series portal](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/research-series/).

### Geographic detail

BLS’s overview describes indexes for:

- The U.S. city average.
- Four Census regions.
- Nine Census divisions.
- Population-size groupings and region/size combinations.
- Twenty-three published local areas.

**Collection areas and publication areas are different concepts.** BLS’s traditional sample has included 75 urban collection areas, but not every sampled area receives its own published local CPI.

The CPI is not a complete state, county, or municipality-level dataset. Local availability and frequency must be checked series by series.

Source: [CPI overview](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/overview.htm).

### Expenditure categories

The principal broad groups are:

1. Food and beverages.
2. Housing.
3. Apparel.
4. Transportation.
5. Medical care.
6. Recreation.
7. Education and communication.
8. Other goods and services.

Numerous detailed indexes and special aggregates are also available, including energy, services, shelter, and **all items less food and energy**, commonly called “core CPI.”

Core CPI does not replace the all-items index and does not imply that food and energy are unimportant household expenses.

### What is included or excluded?

CPI covers consumer goods and services, including applicable sales and excise taxes and user fees. It excludes income taxes and investment assets such as stocks and bonds.

Owner-occupied housing is represented principally through **owners’ equivalent rent**, an estimate of housing-service consumption—not through a house-sale-price index or a direct measure of mortgage payments.

### Units and reference bases

Many CPI-U and CPI-W series use **1982–84 = 100**, but others use different bases. C-CPI-U’s standard base is **December 1999 = 100**.

An index value of 300 is not a dollar price. It expresses a price level relative to a designated reference period.

**A reference base is not the same thing as an expenditure-weight period.** Changing the display base rescales an index; updating expenditure weights changes the construction of subsequent estimates.

---

## 4. History and methodological evolution

CPI’s origins lie in early BLS cost-of-living research and the need to understand price increases affecting workers, especially during World War I.

A useful chronology is:

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| **1917–1919** | Family-expenditure research in industrial centers helped establish early spending weights |
| **1919** | Publication of separate indexes for 32 cities began |
| **1921** | Regular publication of a national U.S. city-average index began; historical estimates extended back to 1913 |
| **1940** | First comprehensive revision: updated expenditure weights and weighted city aggregation |
| **1953** | Broader city coverage, revised items, expanded housing sample, and improved methods |
| **1964** | Another comprehensive redesign |
| **1978** | CPI-U introduced; older worker index renamed CPI-W; probability sampling expanded |
| **1983/1985** | Rental-equivalence treatment of owner-occupied housing adopted for CPI-U/CPI-W |
| **1987** | Updated samples and redesigned housing survey |
| **1998** | Major geographic, item-classification, collection, and estimation revisions |
| **1999** | Geometric-mean formulas introduced for most basic indexes; historical research series introduced |
| **2002** | Chained CPI introduced; biennial expenditure-weight updates began |
| **2007** | Index publication moved to three decimal places |
| **2018** | Geographic revision based on the 2010 Census; Census-division publication introduced |
| **2019–2020** | Consumer Expenditure Survey information replaced the Telephone Point-of-Purchase Survey as the main outlet-frame source |
| **2023** | Expenditure weights began updating annually using one calendar year of spending data |
| **2025–2026** | Collection reductions and shutdown-related missing observations created important documentation and continuity issues |
| **2028, planned** | Geographic sample revision based on the 2020 Census is scheduled to begin |

Source: [BLS chronology of CPI changes](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/historical-changes.htm).

### Why history matters

A century-long CPI series is **not a century of identical measurement practices**. Coverage, weights, sampling, housing treatment, quality adjustment, and formulas have changed.

For long-run research, preserve and consult:

- Official historical CPI.
- The **CPI-U Research Series (CPI-U-RS)**, which incorporates many later methodological improvements into historical estimates.
- Methodological change dates.
- Geographic and item-classification crosswalks.

Do not silently replace the legally used historical CPI with a research reconstruction.

---

## 5. How the CPI is produced

### Sampling and data collection

The CPI combines several linked samples:

1. **Geographic areas**, selected using Census information.
2. **Outlets**, identified through household shopping and expenditure information.
3. **Specific goods and services**, selected within outlets.
4. **Rental housing**, collected through a separate housing survey.

The BLS Handbook overview describes approximately **94,000 price quotes and 8,000 rental-unit quotes each month**. Other overview pages describe about 23,000 establishments and a larger total housing sample.

These counts refer to different units and collection cycles. They should not be treated as contradictory counts of the same thing—or as guaranteed current achieved sample sizes after the 2025 reductions.

Sources: [Handbook overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/home.htm), [CPI overview](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/overview.htm).

### Weights

Expenditure weights describe how much the target population spends on different categories.

Since January 2023, BLS has updated CPI-U and CPI-W spending weights **annually**, using expenditure data from two years earlier. Thus, the official January 2026 indexes introduced weights based on **2024 expenditures**.

BLS estimates that annual updating reduced the average expenditure-data lag from approximately 36 months to 24 months.

Sources: [weight documentation](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/home.htm), [2026 weight comparison](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/relative-importance/weight-update-comparison-2026.htm).

### Aggregation

At a simplified level:

- Most basic indexes use geometric-mean calculations, allowing some substitution within categories.
- CPI-U and CPI-W aggregate categories using a modified Laspeyres framework.
- Final C-CPI-U uses a Törnqvist formula incorporating expenditure shares from adjacent periods.

The actual calculation contains category-specific exceptions and specialized housing procedures. Exact replication requires more than applying a single formula to public tables.

Source: [Handbook calculation chapter](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/calculation.htm).

### Quality adjustment and replacements

Products disappear, change package size, or gain and lose features. BLS uses direct comparison, explicit quality adjustments, hedonic methods in selected categories, and imputation procedures to distinguish price change from changes in what is purchased.

This makes CPI different from simply averaging observed sticker prices.

### Average prices are a separate product

BLS expressly advises using average prices to study **price levels in a particular month**, not as the preferred measure of inflation over time.

An average can change because the mix of products or outlets changes. CPI indexes are designed to measure price change while addressing comparability and quality.

Source: [average-price technical documentation](https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ap/ap.txt).

---

## 6. Publication schedule, revisions, and corrections

### Publication

National CPI is normally released monthly at **8:30 a.m. Eastern Time**, following the reference month, on a preannounced schedule.

Some local indexes are published every other month. Use the official release calendar rather than assuming a fixed day each month.

### Revision policies

| Product | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Not-seasonally-adjusted CPI-U and CPI-W | Generally final when first issued, except corrections |
| Seasonally adjusted CPI-U and CPI-W | Revised when seasonal factors are updated; the usual revision window covers the preceding five years |
| C-CPI-U | Initial estimates are revised as expenditure information becomes available |
| Research products | May be revised or updated under their own methodologies |

**“Final when issued” does not mean “immune from correction.”** BLS publishes errata and correction notices separately from routine statistical revisions.

Sources: [CPI FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers.htm), [seasonal-adjustment FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/seasonal-adjustment/questions-and-answers.htm), [CPI notices](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/notices/).

### Preservation implication

Retain both:

- **Current historical data**, for analysis using the latest estimates.
- **Release-time versions**, for studying what users actually knew on a particular date.

A current database download cannot by itself reconstruct every earlier release.

---

## 7. Important recent disruptions and forthcoming changes

### A. Collection reductions in 2025

BLS’s July 29, 2025 notice states that:

- Collection was suspended entirely in **Lincoln, Nebraska, and Provo, Utah**, beginning in April.
- Collection was suspended entirely in **Buffalo, New York**, beginning in June.
- Roughly **15% of the sample in the other 72 areas** was suspended, on average.
- Both commodities/services and housing collection were affected.

BLS simulated the complete-area suspensions back to 2018. For January 2019–May 2025, the simulated national all-items CPI-U 12-month changes differed from published estimates by less than 0.01 percentage point on average.

**That finding must not be generalized too far.** It addressed the specified three-area simulation, not a complete evaluation of all collection reductions. BLS also said it had not measured the impacts on subnational and item indexes.

Source: [More information on CPI collection reductions](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/notices/2025/more-information-collection-reduction.htm).

### B. Missing October 2025 observations

BLS reports that CPI data were not collected from **October 1 through November 12, 2025**, during a lapse in appropriations.

Consequences included:

- Cancellation of the October 2025 CPI release.
- No published October all-items or all-items-less-food-and-energy estimate.
- Some October series could be published using nonsurvey sources.
- Missing one-month November changes where October observations were unavailable.
- Further effects on housing calculations in April 2026.

**Do not encode the missing October headline observation as zero inflation.** If an analysis imputes it, label that value as researcher-created, not an official BLS observation.

Sources: [revised release dates and CPI explanation](https://www.bls.gov/bls/2025-lapse-revised-release-dates.htm), [shutdown impact on CE and CPI](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/additional-resources/2025-federal-government-shutdown-impact-cpi.htm).

### C. Missing expenditure-survey data

Missing CE collection in October and November 2025 also affects inputs for:

- The 2025 annual CE estimates.
- Final revisions of 2025 chained CPI.
- 2027 CPI-U and CPI-W weights.

BLS reports choosing a survey-weight-adjustment approach after analysis and public expert panels. Preservation should include the methodological explanations and panel documentation, not just the eventual indexes.

### D. Planned 2028 geographic revision

BLS announced a geographic update beginning with January 2028 indexes. It will reflect the 2020 Census and introduce new non-self-representing primary sampling units in waves.

This is a **planned revision**, not a change already implemented.

Source: [2028 geographic revision notice](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/notices/2026/geographic-revision.htm).

---

## 8. Typical users and public benefits

| User community | Typical application | Public significance |
|---|---|---|
| Social Security administrators and beneficiaries | CPI-W cost-of-living adjustments | Helps protect benefit purchasing power |
| Tax administrators and taxpayers | Inflation-adjusted brackets and other statutory amounts | Limits inflation-driven increases in tax burdens |
| Government benefit programs | Eligibility and payment adjustments | Helps maintain the real value of assistance |
| Federal Reserve and economic policymakers | Inflation analysis | Informs monetary and economic policy |
| Treasury and investors | Inflation-indexed securities and inflation-risk assessment | Supports market pricing and financing |
| Employers and labor unions | Wage escalation and bargaining | Provides a shared benchmark |
| Landlords, tenants, and businesses | Contract and rent adjustments | Reduces ambiguity when clauses identify the correct series |
| Researchers and data scientists | Deflation, forecasting, real-income analysis | Separates nominal growth from purchasing-power changes |
| Journalists and educators | Inflation reporting and economic literacy | Makes economic conditions understandable |
| Community and policy advocates | Purchasing-power and affordability analysis | Supports evidence-based scrutiny of policy |

BLS states that CPI applications directly affect **hundreds of millions of Americans**.

Source: [Handbook overview](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/home.htm).

### Public benefits—and distributional consequences

The CPI provides a common, openly accessible benchmark that would be expensive and difficult for individual organizations to reproduce.

But the choice of index is consequential:

- CPI-W is not a retiree-specific index, even though it determines Social Security COLAs.
- Chained CPI can grow differently from CPI-U because of its substitution treatment.
- National averages can conceal substantial differences in household spending patterns.
- Contract escalation benefits one party while increasing another party’s payment obligation.

Thus, **producing a statistical measure and choosing how to use it are separate decisions**. BLS measures price change; lawmakers and contracting parties determine the consequences attached to it.

## 9. Limitations and common misinterpretations

### Population and distribution

CPI-U does not cover everyone. Its target population excludes, among others, rural nonmetropolitan populations, farm households, military installations, and institutional populations.

Even within its coverage, the CPI is not a personalized inflation measure. Renters, homeowners, older adults, low-income households, and households with high medical expenses can experience different price changes.

Expenditure weighting also means CPI is not simply an equal-weighted average of each person’s inflation experience.

### Geography

**Local CPI levels cannot be used to compare the cost of living between cities.** They measure change relative to each area’s own reference period.

For spatial price-level comparisons, consider other products, such as BEA regional price parities.

Source: [CPI FAQ addendum](https://www.bls.gov/cpi/questions-and-answers-addendum.htm).

### Housing

Owners’ equivalent rent measures housing services. It is not a house-price index, a mortgage-affordability index, or an immediate measure of asking rents on newly advertised properties.

### Scope

CPI is not:

- A complete household budget.
- A measure of poverty adequacy.
- A measure of total well-being.
- A producer-price index.
- The GDP price index.
- The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index.

For example, the Federal Reserve’s stated inflation objective is expressed using PCE inflation, although CPI is an important input to its analysis.

### Statistical uncertainty

CPI estimates have sampling and nonsampling error. Detailed and local estimates generally have less precision than the national all-items index.

Potential problems include nonresponse, missing prices, replacements, quality adjustment, expenditure-data error, and changes in purchasing behavior.

**Three decimal places are publication precision, not proof of three-decimal accuracy.**

## 11. Confidential microdata, reuse rights, and access barriers

### Public aggregates versus underlying observations

BLS does not publicly release the full sampled price observations, store identities, or identifiable respondent information. It also does not confirm whether a particular store, brand, or product is in the sample.

Some indexes may be suppressed to protect respondents.

Source: [CPI data sources and confidentiality](https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/cpi/data.htm).

### Restricted research access

BLS documents CPI restricted data extending back to **1989**. However, the dataset-availability table consulted for this report marks CPI **“Access Suspended.”**

Therefore, it would be misleading to promise that a researcher can currently obtain CPI microdata simply by applying. Check with BLS before designing a project dependent on these records.

Where access is offered, institutional agreements, confidentiality training, secure environments, and output review are relevant requirements.

Sources: [restricted-data description](https://www.bls.gov/rda/data/restricted-data.htm), [current availability table](https://www.bls.gov/rda/what-datasets-are-available.htm).

### Reuse rights

BLS states that its published material is in the **public domain**, except previously copyrighted photographs and illustrations.

- Statistical data can be copied, redistributed, and analyzed without special permission.
- BLS asks users to cite it as the source.
- Agency emblems are protected separately.
- Public-domain aggregate data status does not override confidential-microdata restrictions.

Source: [BLS copyright information](https://www.bls.gov/opub/copyright-information.htm).

## 12. Data-science practices for defensible analysis

### Essential checks

1. **Select the correct population:** CPI-U, CPI-W, chained CPI, or research index.
2. **Select the correct geography and category.**
3. **Record seasonal-adjustment status.**
4. **Check the base period and publication frequency.**
5. **Inspect footnotes, missingness, and correction notices.**
6. **Distinguish monthly change, year-over-year change, and annual-average change.**
7. **Save the retrieval date and publication version.**
8. **Do not assume all historical methods are constant.**

### Basic calculations

For index \(I_t\):

\[
\text{Percent change}=100\left(\frac{I_t}{I_{t-k}}-1\right)
\]

Use \(k=1\) for a monthly comparison and \(k=12\) for a year-over-year comparison, provided the necessary observations exist.

To express a nominal amount from period \(t\) in period \(b\) dollars:

\[
\text{Amount in period }b\text{ dollars}
=
\text{Nominal amount}_t\frac{I_b}{I_t}
\]

Match the deflator period to the underlying amount. Annual income is normally paired with an annual index measure, not arbitrarily with December CPI.

### Pipeline safeguards

- Preserve identifiers as strings.
- Parse the actual delimiters and headers; do not hard-code obsolete layouts.
- Keep raw input unchanged alongside normalized data.
- Handle API numeric values returned as strings.
- Detect duplicate observations when combining overlapping bulk partitions.
- Do not interpolate bimonthly series without labeling the result.
- Do not treat absent or suppressed observations as zero.
- Keep research imputations separate from official observations.
- For forecasting or backtesting, use release-time data where necessary to avoid using information unavailable at the historical decision date.

## 13. Preservation priorities and recommended archive design

The following are recommendations, not claims that BLS already provides this complete preservation package.

### Highest-priority preservation package

**A. Published observations**

Acquire CPI-U, CPI-W, C-CPI-U, average prices, relevant research series, and discontinued series needed for continuity.

**B. Metadata**

Preserve all series, area, item, period, and footnote files. Include units and reference bases.

**C. Weights**

Retain expenditure weights, relative-importance tables, weight-update comparisons, and category crosswalks.

**D. Methodology**

Archive all Handbook chapters, technical notes, sampling descriptions, quality-adjustment documentation, and seasonal-factor files.

**E. Publication versions**

Save each release’s HTML, PDF where available, downloadable tables, API responses, and bulk snapshots.

**F. Administrative context**

Retain notices, corrections, shutdown explanations, OMB clearance packages, and planned-revision announcements.

### Recommended preservation controls

- Timestamp snapshots in UTC.
- Preserve source URLs and retrieval logs.
- Compute checksums such as SHA-256.
- Maintain immutable raw files and documented transformations.
- Preserve web pages in WARC or another suitable web-archive format.
- Retain multiple copies in independent storage locations.
- Check record counts, time coverage, unexpected missingness, and changes to metadata.
- Assign version-specific repository identifiers to deposited snapshots.
- Record whether a snapshot contains original releases, corrected observations, or revised seasonal estimates.

### Key preservation risks

| Risk | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Live historical files change | Earlier values can be overwritten by revisions or corrections |
| Metadata is omitted | Numeric values become difficult or impossible to interpret |
| Methods are revised | Long-run comparisons can conceal measurement changes |
| Geographic definitions change | Similar names may refer to different boundaries or samples |
| Missing data is silently filled | Research-created values can be mistaken for official statistics |
| Funding and staffing disruptions | Observation loss cannot necessarily be repaired later |
| Confidential inputs remain unavailable | Public files alone cannot fully reproduce the production process |
| Third-party copies lack provenance | Useful mirrors may differ in timing, transformations, or completeness |

**Preservation judgment:** Archiving only the headline national CPI series is inadequate. The explanatory record is essential to preserving the meaning of the data.

## 14. Policy-accountability questions and research gaps

For activists, oversight bodies, and librarians, productive questions include:

- Are sample reductions affecting local and detailed indexes disproportionately?
- Are achieved collection counts and response rates adequately documented over time?
- Which populations are poorly represented by the principal indexes?

- Are methodological changes documented early enough for users to adapt?
- Are publication versions and corrections easily recoverable?
- What conditions would permit restoration of suspended restricted research access?
- How are shutdown-related gaps handled in contracts and statutory formulas?

These are accountability questions; the existence of a measurement limitation does not by itself establish misconduct.

## Overall finding

**CPI’s historical public data are relatively well protected, but its continuing collection and publication have experienced material disruptions.** The strongest documented risks are missing observations, reduced collection capacity, paused supplementary products, and leadership disruption—not wholesale deletion of historical CPI.

- Routine, documented revisions from destructive or unexplained alterations.
- Proposed budgets from enacted funding.
- Political allegations from evidence about statistical integrity.

- [January 20, 2025 hiring-freeze memorandum, Federal Register](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/28/2025-01905/hiring-freeze): imposed executive-branch hiring restrictions and directed workforce reduction planning.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

Under the rubric’s broad administration-priorities clause, implemented workforce restrictions and consequential collection changes justify High Risk. **Confidence is moderate**, because BLS’s notices identify resource constraints rather than explicitly attributing every reduction to a particular presidential action.

Under a narrower interpretation requiring a **CPI-specific policy directive**, Moderate Risk would be the better classification. I did not identify a presidential-action-driven CPI ICR; the reviewed renewal is described as an ordinary extension.

## Implications for preservation and reliable access

**Wholesale disappearance of already published headline CPI appears less likely than further losses in collection, detail, or supplementary publication.** Statutory uses and extensive redistribution provide protection.

The [Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis’s FRED copy](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL) remained accessible and included observations through August 2026. That demonstrates a separate access route for a major series, **not a complete backup of the entire CPI collection**.

Priority actions:

1. Preserve bulk data **with metadata, footnotes, weights, and methods**.
2. Preserve dated releases and revision versions, especially rebased and seasonally adjusted series.
3. Archive paused research products and discontinued collection-mode tables.
4. Monitor sample restoration, ICR renewal decisions, staffing, and reorganization proposals.
5. Keep missing October 2025 observations explicitly missing. **No mirror can recover an official estimate that was never produced.**
